question: Has anyone from the vendor given inconsistent answers about the product?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every factual claim OrbitFlow staff make about the product: plans/tiers and what each includes, features, connectors/integrations, security/compliance, pricing, roadmap, and capabilities, including hedges, qualifications, and corrections. Quote the speaker's role and the exact wording where possible, and note any statement that is later retracted, changed, or contradicted within the same call.
assumptions: 'Inconsistent answers' is interpreted as contradictions in the vendor's product claims, across or within calls; a single call cannot show cross-call inconsistency, so the reader extracts the underlying statements for later comparison.
No call types restricted because the question concerns the vendor across all calls.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month, that's up to thirty users, annual agreement. Enterprise is custom — that's where the governance and security capabilities sit, plus higher usage.
findings.context: Growth plan starts at $1,800/month for up to thirty users on an annual agreement; Enterprise is custom and holds the governance and security capabilities plus higher usage. — Initial pricing/tier statement by AE Maya Chen, given before user model was discussed.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I don't want to give you a number before I know your user model, because that's exactly where proposals become misleading.
findings.context: Vendor refused to give an exact user count or price until the user model is known; pricing will be itemised. — Later pricing deferral; contrasts with the earlier tier figures, and the Growth tier price was not restated or qualified after this.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users. Approval-only or notification-only can be structured differently depending on the package.
findings.context: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users; approval-only or notification-only users may be structured differently depending on package. — Licensing model statement; qualified as package-dependent.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Baseline is SOC 2 Type II. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Audit logs cover administrative and workflow events. Retention configurable within supported ranges. EU residency available on Enterprise if you ever need it.
findings.context: Enterprise tier includes SAML SSO and SCIM, and EU residency is available on Enterprise; baseline is SOC 2 Type II. — Security/compliance claims by SE Jon Bell; tier-gated features.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Enterprise customers can disable AI features outright. We log the model configuration used for a run. And we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
findings.context: AI can be disabled outright on Enterprise; admins can restrict allowed models; customer workflow content is not used to train a shared model (to be put in contract). — AI governance claims; Enterprise-only disable, and training-use commitment was later deferred to contract.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Noted, and agreed — that belongs in the contract, not on a call.
findings.context: Non-training of customer data was to be documented in the contract rather than asserted on the call. — Vendor AE hedged the earlier verbal assurance by moving it to contract.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: We cache metadata but refresh it, and mapping errors surface on the run.
findings.context: Mapping errors surface on the run and error-rate alerts are available; vendor recommends explicit validation for high-impact flows. — Schema-change handling claim with hedge.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: On Enterprise you can package reusable JavaScript steps if you need to. There's a generic REST action and webhooks. We don't claim every workflow is no-code.
findings.context: Vendor says it does not claim every workflow is no-code; an engineer can supply a custom component, and Enterprise can package reusable JavaScript steps. — Technical capability qualification by SE Jon Bell.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: I'd flag that exact field-level masking requirements should be part of security design rather than something I promise now. We do support role-based access, workspace separation
findings.context: Exact field-level masking is not promised now; should be part of security design. Role-based access and workspace separation are supported. — Hedge on security capability.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: If your policy is strict, AI can be disabled, or we scope the pilot to deterministic steps while security reviews model usage separately.
findings.context: Vendor said AI is optional steps and may be disabled, and said model vs. rules is per use case; later said AI could be scoped out of pilot pending security review. — Vendor scoping hedge on AI, offered as alternative to block security review.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And the run history persists
findings.context: Exception queues can be owned by a group, and person resolved dynamically or via on-call fallback; run history persists with inputs and steps. — Capability claim in response to Tom Alvarez's question on team ownership.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: validate each required operation rather than just point at a logo on our integrations page.
findings.context: Integration reliability for the customer's stack is to be validated in pilot per required operation, not assumed from integrations page; workflows can call private internal APIs only after validation, possibly needing an agent or gateway. — Connector claims hedged; contrasts with the earlier sense of ready-made connectors.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: we're not trying to replace every integration platform. Plenty of our customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep systems integration
findings.context: Vendor stated it is not trying to replace every iPaaS; customers keep iPaaS for deep integration and use OrbitFlow for business-owned workflows. — Positioning statement relevant to Workato overlap.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Yes, all of that under the normal process, and we can complete your questionnaire.
findings.context: Vendor said it would not claim exact security/data-residency needs yet and will provide SOC 2 report, subprocessor list, DPA and architecture docs. — Security documentation commitment.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: SOC 2 Type II is the baseline. SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, both on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Audit logs covering administrative and workflow events. Retention configurable within supported ranges. EU data residency available on Enterprise.
findings.context: OrbitFlow baseline security: SOC 2 Type II; SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning available only on Enterprise; encryption in transit and at rest; audit logs covering administrative and workflow events; EU data residency available on Enterprise. — Stated as baseline capabilities in the security Q&A. Jon gave this list without caveats on the call.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Default depends on where the workspace is provisioned. I'd rather confirm the specifics in writing than guess at your architecture on a call.
findings.context: Default data region depends on where the workspace is provisioned; Jon declined to confirm the specifics on the call and deferred to writing. — Hedge on the EU/US residency question, which Elliot said matters because BrightPath is a US operation with a UK subsidiary.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'm not going to give you a yes on this call. What I will do is get you a written answer from our legal and compliance side within
findings.context: OrbitFlow will not give a yes on a BAA on this call; a written position from legal and compliance was promised within about a week. — Maya's commitment after Elliot said the BAA is a gate. Jon confirmed the one-week timeline.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Configurable within supported ranges. Per-workspace granularity I'd want to check against your specific requirement, because there are limits.
findings.context: Retention is configurable within supported ranges, but per-workspace granularity needs checking because there are limits; the retention floor was not quoted. — Qualified answer. Jon said the limits would go in the pack rather than be stated on the call.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Workspace separation is supported, and Enterprise has stronger governance around who can publish where.
findings.context: Workspace separation is supported; Enterprise has stronger governance over who can publish where. Logical separation was judged supportable. — Jon asked whether separate data planes or logical workspaces were meant. Priya and Elliot said logical was probably enough, and Jon agreed.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Honest answer, it depends on configuration and provider, so I don't want to over-generalise.
findings.context: AI behaviour depends on configuration and provider. Options for strict customers are to disable AI entirely or to scope phase one to deterministic steps and review model usage separately. — Hedged answer ('I don't want to over-generalise'). Elliot chose the phased option, and Maya confirmed that AI off for phase one is not ruled out permanently.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: AI steps here are explicit, inspectable workflow steps. They're not ambient. Admins restrict which models are allowed, Enterprise can disable the features entirely, and we log the model configuration used on each run.
findings.context: AI steps are explicit, inspectable workflow steps. Admins can restrict allowed models, Enterprise can disable AI features entirely, and the model configuration used on each run is logged. — Follow-up to the AI question. Jon described these as product controls.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: We also don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
findings.context: OrbitFlow does not use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model. — Elliot asked whether this is in the contract or only on a marketing page. Maya said it needs to be in the contract for the customer to rely on it.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Role-based access, workspace separation, and secrets are never displayed in run logs.
findings.context: Role-based access and workspace separation control who sees run data; secrets are never displayed in run logs; support access is controlled and logged. Field-level masking is a design conversation, not a standard checkbox. — Jon first described masking as a design item, then said it is designable 'with design'. Both statements are hedged.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: It's designable, I just don't want to say 'yes, masking, done' when the real answer is 'yes, with design'.
findings.context: Field-level masking is 'designable', not an out-of-the-box yes; Jon refused to say 'yes, masking, done'. — Qualification of the masking capability. Elliot needs it so admins can see a step failed without seeing record contents.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Run events and metrics via APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise.
findings.context: Run events and metrics are available via APIs and webhooks, and audit export is available on Enterprise. — Answer to Elliot's question about exporting audit logs to a SIEM. Jon said several customers forward failures to incident tooling.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: A workflow can start from a SaaS event, a schedule, a webhook, a database query, or another workflow.
findings.context: Workflows support SaaS event, schedule, webhook, database query, and workflow triggers. Retries, timeouts, and exception queues are available. Queues can route to a group or resolve a person dynamically, and run history persists. — Product capability descriptions given during the build demo and discussion of ownership of exceptions.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: We don't claim every workflow is no-code.
findings.context: Mapping and branching are visual. Transformations use expressions. Reusable JavaScript steps can be packaged on Enterprise. There is a generic REST action and webhooks. OrbitFlow does not claim every workflow is no-code. — Jon was candid here, qualifying the no-code claim, after Priya asked how technical the tool is.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: For your stack it's a mix of native connectors and API-based options. In a pilot I'd want to validate each required operation rather than pointing at a logo on our integrations page.
findings.context: Integrations are a mix of native connectors and API-based options. Each required operation must be validated in a pilot rather than assumed from the integrations page. Databricks is API work, not impossible. — Jon hedged on connector coverage. Priya said Databricks is not phase one.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month for up to thirty users on an annual agreement. Enterprise is custom-priced
findings.context: Growth plan starts at 1,800 per month for up to 30 users on an annual agreement. Enterprise is custom-priced and includes advanced governance, security capabilities, and higher usage. Given the list, BrightPath is an Enterprise conversation. — Pricing and tier claims. Priya said she was not ready to react, and procurement will not discuss price until the BAA is answered.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed ones. Approval-only or notification-only can be structured differently depending on package.
findings.context: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed seats. Approval-only or notification-only users can be structured differently depending on package. No figure was quoted until the user model is known. — Priya asked what counts as a user. Maya deliberately gave no number.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Yes — you can alert when error rates cross a threshold.
findings.context: Vendor says the workflow builder can alert on error rates crossing a threshold (not per individual failure). — Product capability claim in response to Sophie's request for failure-rate alerting; stated affirmatively.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I believe the Shopify integration is native and event-driven, but I'm not going to swear to the exact trigger coverage without checking.
findings.context: Vendor says the Shopify integration is native and event-driven, but explicitly declines to confirm exact trigger coverage and promises a written answer later. — Hedged connector claim; vendor says the question is for the solutions engineer, not himself.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. On Growth, I'd need to confirm the default processing region for you in writing rather than guess.
findings.context: Vendor says EU data residency is available on Enterprise; on Growth the default processing region is unconfirmed and will be confirmed in writing. — Security/compliance and plan-tier claim; vendor hedged on Growth tier.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month, up to thirty users, on an annual agreement.
findings.context: Vendor states Growth plan pricing starts at £1,800 a month (customer converts to $21.6k/year), up to 30 users, on an annual agreement. — Pricing claim; customer later restates it as 'twenty-one, six' annually, and vendor did not correct it.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I'd be lying if I said it halves it. It's a meaningful discount, not a transformation.
findings.context: Vendor says an annual prepay gives a meaningful discount but does not halve the price. — Pricing/discount hedge; vendor walked back any implication of large savings.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: It's not that we do things Zapier can't. It's that sixty independent Zaps is sixty things to maintain and this is more like eight.
findings.context: Vendor says reusable subflows/templates let sixty automations be maintained as roughly eight, and that the product is not doing things Zapier cannot. — Feature/capability comparative claim versus Zapier, made in response to the sixty-Zap problem.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: That's not extra cost, it's just how it's structured.
findings.context: Vendor says version history and change metadata exist on every workflow, and publish-to-production versus dev-workspace permissions can be defined; a dev workspace is included at no extra cost. — Features/pricing claim; vendor asserted no extra cost for dev workspace without a stated tier qualifier.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connectors. I'd want to model that for your volumes rather than say "no" and surprise you later.
findings.context: Vendor describes AI steps as optional workflow steps (classification, summarisation, field extraction, drafting for human approval), not an autonomous agent, and says usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connectors with pricing to be modelled later. — Feature and pricing claim; vendor says cost will be modelled and put in writing rather than stated.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Then let me put the assumptions in writing and you can hold me to them.
findings.context: Vendor said a per-workflow-run and premium-connector usage model could add cost beyond base pricing, and that it would be confirmed in writing. — Pricing hedge; vendor deferred exact costs.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Those are the two I dodged.
findings.context: Vendor states that the Shopify trigger coverage and default processing region answers were dodged and will be provided in writing. — Self-acknowledged deferral of product claims; confirms earlier hedges were deliberate.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning — both supported, both on Enterprise.
findings.context: OrbitFlow states SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are both supported and both available on Enterprise. — Security/compliance claim made in the governance section, in direct response to the customer's list.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Audit logs cover administrative and workflow events.
findings.context: OrbitFlow states audit logs cover administrative and workflow events. — Stated in the same governance answer as SAML/SCIM; later audit export is claimed for Enterprise (see separate finding).

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: If there are questions we can't answer we'll say "no" rather than "partially".
findings.context: OrbitFlow says it will answer questionnaire items with a plain 'no' rather than 'partially' when it cannot fully answer them. — Maya made this commitment about the 240-question security questionnaire; the customer doubted it.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: What I will not do is tell you there's a one-click SAP connector that solves your estate, because your estate is not one thing.
findings.context: OrbitFlow says there is no one-click SAP connector; SAP connectivity uses API options, a generic REST action, or an agent/gateway for on-premise components. — Vendor hedged the SAP story; this qualifies the earlier, more general 'agent or gateway' answer for on-premise systems.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: So the pattern there is generally an agent or a controlled gateway sitting inside your network that the platform communicates with, rather than direct outbound calls to your systems. But I want to validate that against your actual environment rather than describe it in the abstract.
findings.context: OrbitFlow describes an agent or controlled gateway inside the customer network as the pattern for systems that cannot be reached directly, but says it must be validated against the real environment. — Answer to the customer's requirement that some systems are not exposed to the public internet.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Enterprise customers can disable AI features. Administrators can restrict which models are allowed.
findings.context: OrbitFlow states it can disable AI features on Enterprise, restrict allowed models, and does not use customer workflow content to train a shared model. — Answer to the customer's AI position; the customer said the no-training commitment must be contractual.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise.
findings.context: OrbitFlow states audit export is available on Enterprise, with run events and metrics available via APIs and webhooks. — Answer to the customer's requirement that audit data be exportable; the customer accepted this as satisfactory.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Workspace separation is supported and Enterprise has stronger governance around who can publish where.
findings.context: OrbitFlow says workspace separation is supported with stronger Enterprise governance over publishing, but rollback and promotion patterns vary by workflow and package and are not assumed to map. — Environment separation was a customer requirement; the vendor deliberately qualified the claim.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Field-level masking for specific payloads is a design conversation rather than a checkbox
findings.context: OrbitFlow says field-level masking for specific payloads is a design conversation, not a standard checkbox feature. — Vendor explicitly declined to say 'yes, masking' to avoid a later-discovered gap.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement, but that's not your shape.
findings.context: OrbitFlow says it supports Growth at a list price of 1,800 a month for up to 30 users on an annual agreement, but the customer is an Enterprise deal with custom pricing. — Vendor quoted a Growth price as a reference point, then later declined to give any number for this customer's user model, calling any number misleading.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users. Approval-only or notification-only populations can be structured differently depending on package. I'm not going to give you a number today because without the user model any number is misleading.
findings.context: OrbitFlow says licensed users are builders and full workspace users; approval-only populations may be structured differently; it will not give a number without the user model. — Pricing-model claim made after the customer asked what a 'user' is. Read alongside the earlier Growth price quote, it is a partial answer and not a change of position.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: I'd rather it be answered in writing by someone who can commit to it.
findings.context: OrbitFlow says it cannot yet give a data deletion answer on termination and will provide it in writing. — Deletion on termination was an open customer question; the vendor deferred it to the pack rather than answering on the call.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: It handles it if you build it to. It doesn't handle it by magic.
findings.context: OrbitFlow says it does not 'handle' mid-run contract amendments by default; it must be designed for with re-reading state or a cancellation path. — Vendor qualified an earlier, more general claim that workflows can branch and handle exceptions; the customer noted most vendors say 'yes, it handles that'.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: AI steps are explicit, inspectable steps inside a workflow. They're not ambient and they're not in the execution path unless you put them there. Administrators can restrict which models are allowed. Enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely.
findings.context: AI steps are explicit and not in the execution path unless the customer puts them there; administrators can restrict models and enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely. — Governance answer to Hannah's model-risk gate. Later, T038 says the rule that AI output cannot feed decisions is only a design convention, which is a narrower control than this framing suggests.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: I believe yes, but I want to confirm the exact granularity rather than guess. I'll come back in writing.
findings.context: Per-workspace AI disablement is believed to be supported but the exact granularity is unconfirmed; Nina will confirm in writing. — Hedged answer to Hannah's request for one workspace with AI disabled and another without.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Today it's a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint. I'm not going to tell you there's a switch labelled "AI outputs cannot feed decisions", because there isn't.
findings.context: AI outputs cannot be enforced as leaf nodes by the platform; it is a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint. — Direct correction of the design principle Nina proposed at T036. It sits alongside her T026 claim about controls, and Hannah asked for it to be recorded as a known limitation (T201).

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: SOC 2 Type II is the baseline. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Retention configurable within supported ranges.
findings.context: Security and compliance baseline: SOC 2 Type II, SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise, encryption in transit and at rest, retention configurable within supported ranges. — Answer to Hannah's auditability checklist. Retention is only described as configurable within supported ranges, with no detail given.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: EU data residency available on Enterprise. Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise.
findings.context: EU data residency and audit export are available on the Enterprise tier; run events and metrics are available through APIs and webhooks. — Tier-gated claims. They match the Enterprise positioning Leo gives at T145.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: And we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
findings.context: OrbitFlow does not use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model. — Hannah asked whether this was contractual or marketing. Leo said it needs to be contractual and that legal would insist (T045).

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: API and webhook based, so programmatic. Several customers forward failures and audit events into their own tooling continuously rather than pulling reports.
findings.context: Audit export is API and webhook based, so it is programmatic, and customers forward audit events continuously into their own tooling such as a SIEM. — Nina's answer when Hannah asked what exportable means. Hannah said it is satisfactory subject to seeing the payload schema, and Nina committed to sending the schema.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: you get every step, its inputs, its outputs, timing, retries, and any human approval with who approved and when.
findings.context: The run record shows every step with its inputs, outputs, timing, retries and approvals, and a remediated failed run was shown as one record. — Live demo of run history. The demo showed a timed-out step that was retried and then approved after a human edit.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: that's because this approval was configured to collect a structured input. If someone had just clicked approve, there'd be nothing to compare.
findings.context: The original value before a human edit is retained only when the approval was configured to collect a structured input; a plain approve click leaves nothing to compare. — Qualification of the run-history demo. It undercuts the blanket audit claim at T077 and Nina says it depends on workflow design.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: You can run one in isolation with a given input, yes. Whether that meets your definition of a unit test is a different question, and I suspect it doesn't quite.
findings.context: Subflows can be run in isolation with a given input, but this does not meet Hannah's definition of a unit test. — Qualified answer to Hannah's unit-testing question.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: I'm not going to claim we solve it for you. Each run keeps state, retries are visible in the run record, and you can see whether a step executed. But if a downstream system isn't idempotent and you retry a write, you can absolutely create a duplicate.
findings.context: OrbitFlow does not solve idempotency; a retried write to a non-idempotent downstream system can create a duplicate, and the mitigation is customer design. — Answer to the retry-semantics pain point Hannah raised as the Tray PoC's weakness. Nina is explicitly declining to claim a solution.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: We cache metadata but refresh it, and mapping errors surface on the run.
findings.context: Schema changes are handled by caching metadata and refreshing it, with mapping errors surfacing on the run; alerts can fire when error rates cross a threshold. — Answer to Hannah's concern about silently renamed fields. The answer is about detection after the fact, not prevention.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: The others are a mix of native connectors and API options, and I'd validate each required operation in a pilot rather than pointing at logos.
findings.context: Connectors are a mix of native connectors and API options. Required operations should be validated in a pilot rather than taken from the logos, and the internal event bus needs an architecture pattern because it is not reachable from outside. — Response to Noah's stack list. Nina is hedging on connector coverage, and the event bus is a real architecture gap.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement. You're not a Growth shape — you're Enterprise, which is custom priced and adds the advanced governance, the security capabilities, and higher usage.
findings.context: Growth tier is priced at 1800 a month for up to thirty users on an annual agreement. Enterprise is custom priced and adds advanced governance, security capabilities, and higher usage. — Commercial positioning. Noah's forty builders would exceed Growth's thirty-user limit, so Leo says they are an Enterprise shape.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connector needs.
findings.context: Usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connector needs. Leo will not promise a usage cap structure before modelling volumes. — Pricing and overage. Leo declined to say yes to a cap because it might have conditions attached.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users. Approval-only or notification-only populations can be structured differently depending on the package.
findings.context: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users. Approval-only or notification-only users can be structured differently depending on the package, and the proposal will itemise the split. — Per-seat licensing answer to Noah's forty builders and three hundred viewers. Leo declined to quote a number before modelling.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Workspace separation is supported, and Enterprise has stronger governance around who can publish where. There's version history and change metadata on every workflow, so you can see what changed and when. Rollback and promotion patterns vary a bit by package.
findings.context: Workspace separation is supported and Enterprise has stronger publish governance; version history is kept on every workflow, but rollback and promotion patterns vary by package. — Answer to environment separation. Hannah then asked for a change-management scenario to test rollback.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback.
findings.context: Exception queues can route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback; there is an internal fallback mechanism and separate callouts to external incident tooling. — Answer to Noah's question about team ownership and PagerDuty. Nina says operational incidents and business exceptions should be handled differently.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Approvals in OrbitFlow are acceptable for low-risk cases subject to audit export quality, with risk tiering to be defined.
findings.context: Approvals in OrbitFlow are acceptable for low-risk cases subject to audit export quality, with risk tiering still to be defined; high-risk approvals remain in Jira. — Leo's restatement of a scope change that Hannah accepted, so it is a product-scope position rather than a feature claim.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: All of those are native connectors, no problem at all.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said all listed stack tools (HubSpot, Slack, Google Workspace, Asana, Google Sheets) have native connectors. — Vendor response to customer's stack list; no caveat given.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Yeah, all of that's doable.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said the requested HubSpot-to-Asana-to-Slack workflow with date-slip alerting is doable, but admitted the demo environment could not show it and the scheduled alert approach needed an SE check. — Capability claim that was later qualified: alerting on date slips may need two workflows, and architecture unconfirmed.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: It'd be event driven, so when the record changes it fires.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff described the event-driven alerting as firing on record change, then said a scheduled workflow could cover dates passing, but said two workflows was 'possibly' needed and unconfirmed. — Hedged/changed answer on how date-slip alerts work.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: It's — yeah, it's very good.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said the AI summary step can produce the weekly overdue-accounts summary, and when pressed on accuracy said it is 'very good' while only offering that the user can check underlying data. — Customer raised accuracy concern; vendor did not directly answer.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Yeah, so SSO's included on all our plans, that's standard.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said SSO is included on all plans. — Security/plan claim; later the vendor said he was only 'fairly sure' and would confirm, and customer noted competitors treat it as enterprise-only.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: And we're fully GDPR compliant, so that's all covered.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said the platform is fully GDPR compliant. — Compliance claim made in response to customer security questions.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: We don't train on customer data. That's in the terms.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said customer data is not used to train models, stated as being in the terms, and promised a DPA in writing. — Data-use claim; customer asked for written confirmation.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: So our Growth package is eighteen hundred a month, up to thirty users, on an annual agreement.
findings.context: OrbitFlow Growth package is £1,800 per month, up to thirty users, on an annual agreement. — Core pricing claim; customer computed about £21,500 per year.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Yeah, monthly's usually fine, we can sort something out.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff first said monthly billing is 'usually fine' and that he could not see a problem, then said he needed to check with his manager; later he was asked to confirm and said he would check. — Pricing term hedged and unconfirmed; the vendor did not confirm monthly billing on the call.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: The thirty is the package, so the price is the price.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said the thirty-user minimum is part of the package and seats cannot be reduced to ten, then said the price covers the platform rather than seats. — Seat-count pricing claim; the vendor changed framing from fixed package to platform pricing.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: That's fine, it's completely no-code.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said the product is 'completely no-code' and that the workflow setup needs no code for the customer's use case. — Usability claim; customer said they have no IT team and an ops manager would administer it.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: It's completely flexible.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said the pod-level customisation of onboarding is achievable and 'just configuration', and earlier said the product is completely flexible. — Customer had objected that standardisation would meet resistance; vendor framed product as fully flexible.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: We could have you up and running in a couple of weeks.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said they could have the customer up and running in a couple of weeks. — Timeline claim; customer needs it live before a September launch.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Anyone can move data from A to B. We're about the process.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff described the product as a governance, visibility and audit-trail platform, and said it does more than integration tools. — Positioning claim; customer said nobody audits their onboarding, so the audit claim had limited relevance to them.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Exactly. That's exactly it. Zapier's a toy, basically, once you get past —
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff claimed the competitor-style comparison that Zapier is 'a toy' at scale, then accepted the customer's view that Zapier does about eighty percent of what they need. — Vendor disparaged Zapier; customer pushed back and the vendor softened to 'at scale'.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: I moved off that account so I'm not across the detail. But they renewed, I think.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff gave a customer reference story and said a referenced customer renewed, then said he was not sure and would check. — Unverified claim about a past customer outcome; vendor said he moved off the account.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: The system creates the appropriate remediation task, notifies regional operations, and keeps Dynamics updated as the issue changes state.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's workflow for a blocked installation creates the remediation task, notifies regional operations, and keeps Dynamics updated as the issue changes state (the candidate workflow Maya proposed; customer confirmed it matched their need). — Proposed use-case description, not a confirmed capability; Carlos agreed it fit at T024.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: My general understanding is you'd design the workflow so the sync from the mobile app is eventual rather than assumed, and the workflow tolerates delay rather than treating it as failure. But how that's actually built is his answer, not mine.
findings.context: Offline tolerance: Maya's general understanding is the mobile sync would be eventual and the workflow would tolerate delay, but she explicitly defers how it is built to Jon. — Hedged, deferred to the solutions engineer; later Jon gave the detailed pattern.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: The pattern would be that the workflow doesn't poll the device and doesn't assume presence. It reacts to the sync event when it arrives, and separately it has a timeout rule
findings.context: The workflow reacts to device sync events rather than polling, and a timeout rule turns silence into an exception. Runs keep state, can wait without consuming resources, branch on data, pause for approvals, retry actions, and send exceptions to a queue. — Jon's architecture pattern; the customer said they had not built the timeout pattern before (T090). Described as patterns, not a demo.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Each run keeps state, so yes, it can sit in a waiting state without consuming anything or falling over.
findings.context: Each run keeps state so it can sit waiting without consuming anything or falling over. — Product capability claim about run state; not demonstrated on the call.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And the run history persists so you can see the inputs, which steps ran, and where it stopped.
findings.context: Queues can route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call fallback; run history persists showing inputs, steps run, and where it stopped. — Jon said the on-call rota should ideally resolve from the customer's source of truth, which is split between Dynamics and a shared calendar (T098-T100); this was not checked against OrbitFlow's capability.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: There are integration routes to Dynamics — API-based, plus our generic REST action and webhooks. What I'm not going to tell you is that we have the deepest first-class Dynamics connector on the market
findings.context: Dynamics 365 integration routes exist (API-based, a generic REST action, and webhooks), but OrbitFlow does not have the deepest first-class Dynamics connector on the market. This is the key gap versus Power Automate. — Candid admission that the customer called the 'biggest issue'; Maya repeated the gap in her summary (T201).

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: we push people hard towards small reusable subflows rather than one big canvas, and that's the mechanism. But you should make me prove it.
findings.context: Reusability is achieved through small reusable subflows rather than one large canvas; Jon said it should be proven rather than claimed. — Vendor mechanism claim, offered with a proposed test.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise, and Azure AD works with that. Audit logs cover administrative and workflow events.
findings.context: Security: SAML SSO and SCIM are available on Enterprise, Azure AD works with them, and audit logs cover administrative and workflow events. — Stated for Enterprise tier only; the customer's Azure AD requirement was raised at T131.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. UK specifically I'd need to confirm rather than assume, and I'm not going to say yes to make the call go smoothly.
findings.context: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. UK data residency is not confirmed; Jon would confirm it in writing rather than assume. — Customer preferred UK residency (not mandatory, T134). Maya promised a written answer at T195.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Role-based access and workspace separation are the mechanisms. If you want region A to be unable to see region B's runs, that's workspace design plus permissions. It's doable, but how you slice it matters and I'd want to design it rather than assert it.
findings.context: Regional access control uses role-based access and workspace separation, though the design must be worked out rather than asserted. — Customer wanted region-limited access; Jon hedged on how well it fits.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Enterprise supports stronger governance around who can publish where.
findings.context: Enterprise supports stronger governance over who can publish where, with a central group owning standards and publishing rights and regions contributing. — Governance claim tied to the Enterprise tier.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement. Enterprise is custom priced
findings.context: Pricing: Growth tier is £1,800 a month (currency not stated on the call) up to thirty users on an annual agreement; Enterprise is custom priced and includes advanced governance, security capabilities, and higher usage. — Currency was not stated in the transcript; the amount is given only as 'eighteen hundred a month'. Customer said price may be defensible for central operations.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed ones. Approval-only or notification-only populations can be structured differently depending on the package.
findings.context: Licensing: builders and full workspace users are licensed seats; approval-only or notification-only users may be structured differently depending on the package. No seat number was given because the builder-to-approver ratio was unknown. Maya said the shape must be explicit in writing before any internal use. — Customer expects several hundred approvers and six builders, which is a licensing-model concern.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'm not going to pretend we can beat bundled licensing on price.
findings.context: OrbitFlow cannot beat Power Automate's bundled licensing on price; the argument must be operational cost instead. — Concession on cost, not a product capability claim.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: I can talk about architecture patterns in detail, and I can talk about roadmap direction, but I can't commit to roadmap dates.
findings.context: Roadmap: Jon can discuss architecture patterns and roadmap direction, but will not commit to roadmap dates. — Limits on roadmap disclosure; the customer accepted direction without dates (T187).

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: The decisive gap is that Power Automate is embedded and first-class on Dynamics and we're not, so the case has to be operational cost, not licence cost.
findings.context: Maya's summary characterises OrbitFlow's Dynamics position as a decisive gap: Power Automate is embedded and first-class on Dynamics, and OrbitFlow is not. — Summary restating Jon's T104 admission, not a new claim.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise.
findings.context: Enterprise tier includes SAML SSO and SCIM; Growth tier is priced at 1800 a month up to 30 users on an annual agreement; Enterprise is custom priced and needed for everything the customer asked for. — Vendor pricing and tier inclusion stated by AE; SSO/SCIM and audit export are stated as Enterprise features.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement. You're not a Growth shape — everything Samir's asked for sits in Enterprise, which is custom priced.
findings.context: Growth is 1800 a month up to 30 users on an annual agreement; everything the customer asked for sits in Enterprise, which is custom priced. — Commercial tier statement by AE.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: SOC 2 Type II is the baseline. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Audit logs covering administrative and workflow events. Retention configurable within supported ranges. Subprocessor list published with change notification. And we do not use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
findings.context: SOC 2 Type II is the security baseline; encryption in transit and at rest; audit logs for admin and workflow events; retention configurable within supported ranges; subprocessor list with change notification; customer workflow content is not used to train a shared model. — Security/compliance list answering customer's checklist; retention numbers deferred to pack.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. UK specifically I need to confirm in writing. I'm not going to say yes on a call.
findings.context: EU data residency is available on Enterprise; UK residency is unconfirmed and will be confirmed in writing, possibly a gate. Later the vendor committed to a definitive answer within the week. — Hedged; customer pressed EU vs UK distinction.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: We do not have a native concept of a matter-level ethical wall that reads your barrier definitions from iManage and enforces them dynamically. That does not exist.
findings.context: No native matter-level ethical wall that reads information barrier definitions from iManage and enforces them dynamically; this does not exist. Design around it via workspace separation and scoped credentials, which must be maintained as barriers change. — Explicit capability limitation; contrasts with the general role-based access claim.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: native legal-system connectors are limited. In our catalogue, specifically, limited.
findings.context: Native legal-system connectors for iManage and Intapp are limited in the catalogue; integration works through their APIs via generic REST action and webhooks, not a maintained native connector. — Connector capability; vendor said 'limited' and that the work is integration rather than configuration.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Whatever the workflow passes between steps is visible in the run record, yes.
findings.context: Run record holds every step, inputs, outputs, timing, retries and human approval identity and timestamp; pass-through data is visible in run records; secrets never displayed; field-level masking is design not a switch. — Logging and data visibility claims; the vendor first conceded payloads are visible, then said the 'checkbox' does not exist.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise.
findings.context: Audit export to SIEM is on Enterprise; run events and metrics via APIs and webhooks; payload schema to be sent. — Audit export capability; vendor later said the schema would be sent.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Yes. Enterprise customers can disable AI features. Administrators can also restrict which models are allowed if you want a middle position rather than off.
findings.context: Enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely; admins can restrict allowed models. Later said AI-step build permission granularity is unconfirmed ('I believe so'). — AI control claim, hedged in one place and firm in another; the customer asked for it confirmed in the pack.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: I believe so, but that's a permissions-granularity question and I want to confirm it rather than guess.
findings.context: Restricting who can build AI steps separately from workflows generally is believed possible but unconfirmed. — Hedged capability; put on written list.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Connections and credentials are centrally managed and referenced by workflows — a builder uses a connection, they don't see or control the secret.
findings.context: Workflow connections are centrally managed; read-only connection scoping prevents writes; connection scopes can be audited; credentials rotate at connection layer. — Security control claims about credential design.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: If they're publicly reachable with authentication, outbound calls are straightforward. For genuinely private networks it depends on your environment and may require an agent or a controlled gateway.
findings.context: Outbound calls to publicly reachable authenticated internal APIs are straightforward; private networks may need an agent or gateway. — Connectivity capability with environment caveat.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: I would not claim you can export a workflow and run it unchanged somewhere else. You can't.
findings.context: Workflow definitions and run data can be exported via supported APIs; the product is not portable as a runnable workflow elsewhere. — Portability claim with explicit correction of any implied portability.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: And approval forms can collect structured input, so it isn't just yes or no.
findings.context: Approval forms collect structured input and approvals are logged with identity and timestamp; a notification plus optional dashboard design is possible. — Feature claim for approvals.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: On the rest — Microsoft 365, Teams and SharePoint are well-trodden. Azure is fine.
findings.context: Microsoft 365, Teams and SharePoint are well-trodden; Azure is fine; generic REST and webhooks available. — Connector coverage claim.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed ones. Approval-only or notification-only populations can be structured differently depending on package.
findings.context: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed seats; approval-only seats may be structured differently; no per-seat number given. — Licensing claim, explicitly withheld pricing.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I won't dress a roadmap item as a capability.
findings.context: Vendor said a 'no roadmap' stance: will not dress roadmap items as capabilities; the earlier claim that security would be enforced by design, plus the admitted absence of ethical wall, are the main cross-check points. — Roadmap policy statement by AE.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: So this is a workflow that's roughly the pattern we're describing. It's scheduled rather than event-driven — it runs daily, queries the warehouse, joins against the CRM, and evaluates a set of conditions.
findings.context: Workflow runs on a daily schedule, queries the warehouse, joins against the CRM, and evaluates conditions; the query can live in the workflow or in a Snowflake view the customer owns. — Product demo description. Jon hedges the Snowflake option as 'probably better' for this customer, so it is a recommendation rather than a firm capability claim.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Assign it to the account's CSM, or to a queue if the owner field is stale. Escalate if nothing happens in N days.
findings.context: Flagged accounts generate a structured follow-up task, assigned to the CSM or to a queue if the owner field is stale, with escalation if no action within N days. — Jon's description of how the 'act on it' step works. The stale-owner fallback relies on a field Maya had earlier said should not drive logic, a tension the call does not resolve.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Machine-generated usage data and structured ticket data carry the flag. Human-maintained fields are context you show to the person, not inputs the logic depends on.
findings.context: Human-maintained fields should be shown as context to the person, not used as inputs the logic depends on; signals should be weighted by how they are produced. — Maya's design position, later partly contradicted by Jon's reliance on the owner field for routing (T092).

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: You build it. It's a field on the task and a report. I'm not going to tell you there's a built-in model-monitoring feature, because there isn't.
findings.context: Dismissal tracking for false positives is not a built-in feature; the customer must build it as a field on the task and a report. — Jon first offers dismissal tracking as a health metric, then clarifies it is a customer build, not a product feature.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: The way we'd build it is that the source references are stored alongside the generated output, so whoever reads the summary can click through to the tickets that produced each claim.
findings.context: Source references are stored alongside AI-generated output so readers can click through to the tickets behind each claim. — Introduced as 'the way we'd build it', so it is a proposed design rather than a confirmed existing feature.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: What I wouldn't do is rely on the model's own confidence score as a guarantee.
findings.context: The workflow can require a minimum number of supporting tickets before reporting a theme, and thin cases can go to review; the model's own confidence score should not be relied on as a guarantee. — Design guidance about preventing invented themes. It describes what the customer can configure, and Jon explicitly declines to vouch for model confidence.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Administrators can restrict which models are allowed, and Enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely. We log the model configuration used on each run, and we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
findings.context: AI steps are inspectable (prompt, model, configuration); admins can restrict allowed models; Enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely; model configuration is logged per run; customer workflow content is not used to train a shared model. — Security and AI governance claims. The disable-AI option is tier-specific (Enterprise), which Jon states without saying what Growth allows.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: If the view we consume contains no student-level columns, no workflow can leak them regardless of who builds it.
findings.context: Student-level data can be excluded by design: if the Snowflake view has no student-level columns, no workflow can expose them. — Jon's architectural claim, which depends on the customer's view design rather than a built-in control. Maya separately notes the vendor security review still applies.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: SOC 2 Type II baseline, SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise, encryption in transit and at rest, audit logs covering administrative and workflow events, retention configurable within supported ranges.
findings.context: Security baseline includes SOC 2 Type II, encryption, audit logs, configurable retention, and APIs/webhooks; SAML SSO and SCIM and audit export are Enterprise-only. — Jon's list of security capabilities. The tier gating on SSO, SCIM, and audit export matters because Growth is also described as lacking some security capabilities (see T150).

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement.
findings.context: Growth is priced at a fixed monthly rate up to thirty users on an annual agreement; Enterprise is custom-priced and adds advanced governance, security capabilities, and higher usage. — Maya's pricing and tier claim. Tier contents are stated at a high level only.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed ones. Approval-only or notification-only can be structured differently by package.
findings.context: Licensing depends on builders versus recipients; approval-only or notification-only users may be structured differently by package. Maya declines to quote a figure until the split is known. — Maya's hedge on licensing. It qualifies the earlier 'up to thirty users' Growth limit, since the customer has about sixty-two task recipients.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Version history and change metadata are there, so you can see what changed and when. Definitions can be exported through the API.
findings.context: Version history and change metadata are available and definitions can be exported via API, but this is not a git integration and a side-by-side diff is unconfirmed. — Jon's answer on version control. He corrects himself from a possibly broader 'diff' implication to a hedged answer that a diff needs confirming.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Definitions export through the API. It's a structured representation, not an opaque blob.
findings.context: Workflow definitions export through the API as a structured representation, not an opaque blob, but it is OrbitFlow's own schema and not a portable format another engine could execute. — Initial product claim about export; later Nina says definitions are readable and diffable in the text sense, pending real examples she has not yet supplied.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: API and UI both.
findings.context: Definitions can be created and updated through both the API and the UI. — Authoring capability claim; Nina then hedges that she would discourage a repo-as-source-of-truth workflow for the first six months.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Connections and credentials are centrally managed and referenced by workflows. A builder uses a connection; they never see the secret.
findings.context: Connections and credentials are centrally managed and referenced by workflows; builders never see the secret, and rotation happens at the connection layer. — Security/secrets capability claim presented as a well-supported existing pattern.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Secret values are never displayed in run logs. Whatever the workflow passes between steps as data is visible, though
findings.context: Secret values are never displayed in run logs, but data passed between steps is visible, so a token placed in a variable is exposed. — Security claim with a qualification.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connector needs. Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users, annual.
findings.context: Billing unit is scoped on workflow runs and premium connector needs; Growth tier is $1,800 a month up to thirty users, annual; the customer is an Enterprise conversation given the security list. — Pricing claim from Leo. Later Leo and Nina say subflow billing semantics are unconfirmed and promised in writing; Marcus asks about user counting and Leo says builders and full workspace users are licensed.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: I believe subflow invocations are counted, but I'm not going to state the exact billing semantics from memory.
findings.context: Whether a subflow invocation counts as a separate workflow run for billing is not confirmed; Nina believes subflows are counted but will not state exact billing semantics from memory. Leo later says he will answer in writing. — Hedged pricing claim, later reduced to an open item to be answered in writing; the earlier claim that usage is scoped on runs is contingent on this.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: SOC 2 Type II is the baseline. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest.
findings.context: OrbitFlow supports SOC 2 Type II as baseline, SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise, encryption in transit and at rest, audit logs, and EU data residency on Enterprise. — Security/compliance list given in response to customer's requirements; the customer later notes EU residency is a contractual requirement.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: manual re-trigger yes, deterministic replay no.
findings.context: Manual re-trigger of a workflow is available, but a true deterministic replay of a historical run with its original captured state is not supported. — Capability clarified after the customer asked about replay; Nina explicitly separates the two to avoid conflation.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Near real-time via webhook. I don't want to quote you a millisecond figure.
findings.context: Run events are available through a run events API and near-real-time webhooks; Nina declined to quote a latency figure. — Observability capability claim; latency left unquantified.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: They're documented. There are platform limits and retry controls, and you can design throttling patterns.
findings.context: Platform rate limits are documented and there are retry controls; Nina said the design must be checked against the downstream Salesforce quota. — Limits claim; actual numbers not provided.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: That's scoped on the Salesforce side by the permissions of the user or integration account you connect with. We use what you give us.
findings.context: Permissions for Salesforce access are controlled upstream by the Salesforce user or integration account; OrbitFlow adds no further restriction layer. — Least-privilege claim.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: No. We recommend it. There's no linter.
findings.context: OrbitFlow has no linter for enforcing composition of small reusable subflows; it only recommends the pattern. — Feature gap admitted by Nina, contrasting with the claim that the platform pushes composition.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: I'd suggest pointing it at a read replica for the evaluation regardless.
findings.context: Postgres connector behaviour (connection handling, timeouts) is documented and will be provided; Nina recommends a read replica for evaluation. — Connector claim with deferred documentation.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: But we can't make a non-idempotent API idempotent.
findings.context: Nina said OrbitFlow cannot make a non-idempotent downstream API idempotent; duplicate Salesforce records are possible if a write succeeded but the response was lost, though run records show retries. — Capability limitation stated directly after the customer tested for overclaiming.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: There are retry controls and you can set caps per workflow, and we can look at whether yours are configured sensibly — I suspect two or three of them aren't.
findings.context: Retry controls exist and caps can be set per workflow, but the customer's configuration may be wrong; Ruth suspects two or three workflows are not configured sensibly. — Answer to the customer's question on whether the March retry storm could recur. Ruth hedges with 'partly' and 'I suspect'.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: Instrumentation is light — you're recording state transitions, not orchestrating them. Maybe a few thousand a month.
findings.context: Instrumentation of supplier onboarding is light: it records state transitions rather than orchestrating them, at roughly a few thousand runs a month. — Run-cost estimate for the proposed visibility-only first phase of the supplier onboarding work.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Current contract is Enterprise, nine builder seats, run tier at two hundred and fifty thousand a month. It expires the eighteenth of October.
findings.context: The customer is on the Enterprise plan with nine builder seats and a 250k-per-month run tier, expiring 18 October. — Maya restating current contract terms before the renewal pricing discussion.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: List uplift at renewal is seven percent. That's the standard annual adjustment and I'm not going to pretend it's negotiable in principle — it applies to everyone.
findings.context: The list uplift at renewal is seven percent, applies to all customers, and is not negotiable in principle. — Maya says it is not negotiable in principle, but later says a two-year term lets her fix the year-two uplift, which suggests some flexibility.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: A two-year commitment lets me fix the uplift for year two, which given where inflation's gone is probably worth more than the discount itself.
findings.context: A two-year commitment lets Maya fix the uplift for year two, which she says may be worth more than the discount itself. — Possible tension with the earlier statement that the uplift is not negotiable in principle.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Three fifty gives you about twenty percent headroom on your current trajectory. Four hundred gives you a year and the instrumentation project.
findings.context: The 350k tier gives about 20% headroom on current trajectory; the 400k tier gives a year of headroom plus the instrumentation project. The step from 350k to 400k is a smaller increment than 250k to 350k. — Tier sizing advice. Maya initially says 'I think you should take four hundred' and recommends it over 350k.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: you're looking at roughly nine percent above what you paid this year. If we kept nine seats it'd be closer to fourteen.
findings.context: Directional total: with seven seats, the 7% uplift and the 400k tier, the cost is roughly 9% above this year; with nine seats it would be closer to 14%. — Directional pricing given verbally, with exact numbers promised later in the written proposal.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: the seat reduction is genuine — I'm not inflating the run tier to compensate.
findings.context: The seat reduction is genuine and the run tier is not being inflated to compensate for it. — Maya's assurance to the customer about the pricing structure.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'd do three. Should you? Probably not.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen

draft.answer: Yes. The strongest cases are Alastair McCrae on Fable Media (overclaims later hedged) and Trafford Dental, Maya Chen on pricing and contract terms, Ruth Adeyemi on churn and at-risk calls, and Nina Patel on AI controls [C1][C2][C3][C4][C5][C6]. Some inconsistencies are directly stated, and others are inferred or only appear alongside other statements [C7].

claims.text: Alastair McCrae (Fable Media) made several confident claims that he then hedged or changed. He said SSO is included on all plans, then was only 'fairly sure'. He said monthly billing is 'usually fine', then needed to check with his manager. He said the thirty-user minimum is the package, then said the price covers the platform rather than seats. He said alerting is event-driven, then that two workflows may be needed. He called Zapier 'a toy', then softened. He said a referenced customer renewed, then said he wasn't sure. He also said the product is 'fully GDPR compliant' and 'completely no-code'.
Alastair McCrae (Trafford Dental) said OrbitFlow can integrate with anything that has an API, then said 'I'd have to check' whether the NHS e-Referral system has one.

Ruth Adeyemi (Oakhill Property) said 'There isn't one' regarding a smaller plan than Growth, then asked whether the customer would buy a $500/month five-workflow plan. Alastair McCrae confirmed he had told the customer no smaller plan existed. Ruth also said producing screenshots is not a service offered while offering to arrange it.
