answer.question: Has anyone from the vendor given inconsistent answers about the product?
answer.answer: Yes. The strongest cases are Alastair McCrae on Fable Media (overclaims later hedged) and Trafford Dental, Maya Chen on pricing and contract terms, Ruth Adeyemi on churn and at-risk calls, and Nina Patel on AI controls [1][2][3][4][5][6]. Some inconsistencies are directly stated, and others are inferred or only appear alongside other statements [7].

claims.text: Alastair McCrae (Fable Media) made several confident claims that he then hedged or changed. He said SSO is included on all plans, then was only 'fairly sure'. He said monthly billing is 'usually fine', then needed to check with his manager. He said the thirty-user minimum is the package, then said the price covers the platform rather than seats. He said alerting is event-driven, then that two workflows may be needed. He called Zapier 'a toy', then softened. He said a referenced customer renewed, then said he wasn't sure. He also said the product is 'fully GDPR compliant' and 'completely no-code'.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: Yeah, so SSO's included on all our plans, that's standard.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said SSO is included on all plans. — Security/plan claim; later the vendor said he was only 'fairly sure' and would confirm, and customer noted competitors treat it as enterprise-only.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: Yeah, monthly's usually fine, we can sort something out.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff first said monthly billing is 'usually fine' and that he could not see a problem, then said he needed to check with his manager; later he was asked to confirm and said he would check. — Pricing term hedged and unconfirmed; the vendor did not confirm monthly billing on the call.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: The thirty is the package, so the price is the price.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said the thirty-user minimum is part of the package and seats cannot be reduced to ten, then said the price covers the platform rather than seats. — Seat-count pricing claim; the vendor changed framing from fixed package to platform pricing.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: It'd be event driven, so when the record changes it fires.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff described the event-driven alerting as firing on record change, then said a scheduled workflow could cover dates passing, but said two workflows was 'possibly' needed and unconfirmed. — Hedged/changed answer on how date-slip alerts work.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: Yeah, all of that's doable.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said the requested HubSpot-to-Asana-to-Slack workflow with date-slip alerting is doable, but admitted the demo environment could not show it and the scheduled alert approach needed an SE check. — Capability claim that was later qualified: alerting on date slips may need two workflows, and architecture unconfirmed.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: Exactly. That's exactly it. Zapier's a toy, basically, once you get past —
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff claimed the competitor-style comparison that Zapier is 'a toy' at scale, then accepted the customer's view that Zapier does about eighty percent of what they need. — Vendor disparaged Zapier; customer pushed back and the vendor softened to 'at scale'.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: I moved off that account so I'm not across the detail. But they renewed, I think.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff gave a customer reference story and said a referenced customer renewed, then said he was not sure and would check. — Unverified claim about a past customer outcome; vendor said he moved off the account.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: And we're fully GDPR compliant, so that's all covered.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said the platform is fully GDPR compliant. — Compliance claim made in response to customer security questions.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: That's fine, it's completely no-code.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said the product is 'completely no-code' and that the workflow setup needs no code for the customer's use case. — Usability claim; customer said they have no IT team and an ops manager would administer it.

claims.text: Alastair McCrae (Trafford Dental) said OrbitFlow can integrate with anything that has an API, then said 'I'd have to check' whether the NHS e-Referral system has one.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: We can integrate with anything that's got an API, so —
evidence.context: Vendor claims OrbitFlow can integrate with anything that has an API. — Alastair responding to customer's question about NHS e-Referral integration; a general capability claim about connectors, not verified for this system.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: I'd have to check.
evidence.context: Vendor could not confirm whether the NHS e-Referral system has an API, undercutting the earlier blanket integration claim. — Hedge/retraction within the same call: after claiming integration with anything with an API, vendor said he would have to check whether the customer's referral system has one.

claims.text: Ruth Adeyemi (Oakhill Property) said 'There isn't one' regarding a smaller plan than Growth, then asked whether the customer would buy a $500/month five-workflow plan. Alastair McCrae confirmed he had told the customer no smaller plan existed. Ruth also said producing screenshots is not a service offered while offering to arrange it.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: There isn't one.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff said there is no smaller plan than Growth; the entry point is Growth. — Customer said she was told the entry point is Growth. Ruth's flat denial is later undercut by her own hypothetical about a five-hundred-a-month plan in T126.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: If we did have a smaller plan — five hundred a month, five workflows, three users, no approval forms — would you buy it?
evidence.context: Ruth raised the possibility of a smaller plan at five hundred a month with five workflows, three users and no approval forms, which contradicts her earlier statement that none exists. — Framed as a hypothetical, but it is inconsistent with 'There isn't one' in T065. Ruth then says she will pass the feedback on.

evidence.speaker: Alastair McCrae
evidence.quote: I did say that.
evidence.context: Alastair confirms he told the customer at the time that no smaller plan existed. — Confirms the earlier statement that Growth is the entry point. Customer's T068 quote is from a different speaker and is not part of this quote.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: It's not a thing we offer, but it's eleven workflows and it'll take an hour.
evidence.context: Workflow definitions can be exported through the API, but Ruth then says producing screenshots is not a service OrbitFlow offers, despite having offered to arrange it. — Ruth first points to the API export, then offers a manual screenshot service she describes as not a standard offering.

claims.text: Ruth Adeyemi (Verity Payments) claimed the operating-model guidance says the product does not remove the need for an operations role, then retracted when the customer had never seen it ('Then we don't say it, do we'). Maya Chen separately restated that position as a product stance.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: We do say that, in fairness. It's in the operating model guidance.
evidence.context: The vendor's operating model guidance states that the product does not remove the need for an operations role; it changes what that role must be good at. — Ruth first claimed this is documented, then retracted it when the customer said they had never seen the guidance. The customer had earlier said they believed the product removed the need for such a role.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: Then we don't say it, do we.
evidence.context: Retraction of the operating model guidance claim: the vendor no longer says the guidance exists or that it states this clearly. — Direct self-contradiction within the call, following the earlier claim that the guidance documents this point.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: That the product doesn't remove the need for the role. It changes what the role has to be good at.
evidence.context: The product does not need a dedicated role to succeed, and the vendor's own account manager said it changes the skills required of the role rather than eliminating the role. — Maya restated the customer's point as a product position. Customer had said the product removed the need for a person, which the vendor then contradicted.

claims.text: Maya Chen (Lumen Retail) said the 7% renewal uplift is not negotiable in principle, then said a two-year term lets her fix the year-two uplift. She also said 'I'd do three' years, then that two years is where she'd sit and three is probably not right for the customer.

evidence.quote: List uplift at renewal is seven percent. That's the standard annual adjustment and I'm not going to pretend it's negotiable in principle — it applies to everyone.
evidence.context: The list uplift at renewal is seven percent, applies to all customers, and is not negotiable in principle. — Maya says it is not negotiable in principle, but later says a two-year term lets her fix the year-two uplift, which suggests some flexibility.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: A two-year commitment lets me fix the uplift for year two, which given where inflation's gone is probably worth more than the discount itself.
evidence.context: A two-year commitment lets Maya fix the uplift for year two, which she says may be worth more than the discount itself. — Possible tension with the earlier statement that the uplift is not negotiable in principle.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I'd do three. Should you? Probably not.
evidence.context: On multi-year terms, Maya first says she would do three years, then says two years is where she would sit and that three years is probably not right for the customer. — Self-contradiction within the same call on the recommended term length.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Two years is where I'd sit.
evidence.context: Two years is the recommended term, and Maya says she would sit there, not three. — Follows the earlier 'I'd do three' remark; both statements are reported.

Maya Chen (DeltaWorks) quoted Growth at 1,800/month, then declined to give any number. A finding notes this is a partial answer rather than a change of position.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month, that's up to thirty users, annual agreement. Enterprise is custom — that's where the governance and security capabilities sit, plus higher usage.
evidence.context: Growth plan starts at $1,800/month for up to thirty users on an annual agreement; Enterprise is custom and holds the governance and security capabilities plus higher usage. — Initial pricing/tier statement by AE Maya Chen, given before user model was discussed.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I don't want to give you a number before I know your user model, because that's exactly where proposals become misleading.
evidence.context: Vendor refused to give an exact user count or price until the user model is known; pricing will be itemised. — Later pricing deferral; contrasts with the earlier tier figures, and the Growth tier price was not restated or qualified after this.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement, but that's not your shape.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow says it supports Growth at a list price of 1,800 a month for up to 30 users on an annual agreement, but the customer is an Enterprise deal with custom pricing. — Vendor quoted a Growth price as a reference point, then later declined to give any number for this customer's user model, calling any number misleading.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users. Approval-only or notification-only populations can be structured differently depending on package. I'm not going to give you a number today because without the user model any number is misleading.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow says licensed users are builders and full workspace users; approval-only populations may be structured differently; it will not give a number without the user model. — Pricing-model claim made after the customer asked what a 'user' is. Read alongside the earlier Growth price quote, it is a partial answer and not a change of position.

She later said that AI outputs cannot be enforced as leaf nodes, as it is only a design convention plus review. Leo Grant and Ruth Adeyemi also contributed to inconsistent claims. Ruth (Pinewood) said a workflow has been failing 'every four hours since January', which a finding infers does not match her later 'two thousand times' figure. Jon Bell (Acme Logistics) hedged some claims after giving them, and Maya Chen also hedged her non-training assurance by moving it to the contract.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: AI steps are explicit, inspectable steps inside a workflow. They're not ambient and they're not in the execution path unless you put them there. Administrators can restrict which models are allowed. Enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely.
evidence.context: AI steps are explicit and not in the execution path unless the customer puts them there; administrators can restrict models and enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely. — Governance answer to Hannah's model-risk gate. Later, T038 says the rule that AI output cannot feed decisions is only a design convention, which is a narrower control than this framing suggests.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: Today it's a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint. I'm not going to tell you there's a switch labelled "AI outputs cannot feed decisions", because there isn't.
evidence.context: AI outputs cannot be enforced as leaf nodes by the platform; it is a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint. — Direct correction of the design principle Nina proposed at T036. It sits alongside her T026 claim about controls, and Hannah asked for it to be recorded as a known limitation (T201).

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: It's been failing since January. Every four hours.
evidence.context: The 'TEMP - do not use' workflow has been failing since January, every four hours. — Vendor's account of the failure cadence. Later the same speaker says a workflow failed 'two thousand times', which does not match a four-hourly schedule since January (roughly 1,400 runs by September). Inferred inconsistency in the vendor's figures.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Noted, and agreed — that belongs in the contract, not on a call.
evidence.context: Non-training of customer data was to be documented in the contract rather than asserted on the call. — Vendor AE hedged the earlier verbal assurance by moving it to contract.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: If your policy is strict, AI can be disabled, or we scope the pilot to deterministic steps while security reviews model usage separately.
evidence.context: Vendor said AI is optional steps and may be disabled, and said model vs. rules is per use case; later said AI could be scoped out of pilot pending security review. — Vendor scoping hedge on AI, offered as alternative to block security review.
